name: GW0742

lead: GW0742 is a selective PPAR-delta agonist made by GlaxoSmithKline and used mostly as a lab tool. Some bodybuilding and fat-loss communities market it as a stronger sibling of GW501516.
Published research is cell and animal work on inflammation, metabolism and the heart; no human trials were found.

paras: It activates PPAR-delta, a nuclear receptor involved in fatty acid oxidation, glucose handling and inflammation, in laboratory models.
It is not an approved medicine and human safety data are lacking. Rodent studies of the related GW501516 reported tumour promotion, and that concern is cited for GW0742 as well.

lead: GW0742 (also GW610742 and proposed trade name fitorine) is an investigational PPAR-delta (PPAR-beta/delta) agonist investigated by GlaxoSmithKline and used widely as a laboratory tool compound. It is not an approved medicine.[1][2]

Grokipedia reports that it is sold illicitly to bodybuilders and athletes under names such as "Cardarine 2.0", positioned as an alternative to the related compound GW501516; it also notes concerns, drawn from rodent work on its analogue, about tumour promotion.[2] No human clinical trials were found.

paras: GW0742 is a thiazole-based compound structurally related to GW501516.[2] A 2003 paper from the GSK-linked group described the synthesis and biological activity of novel selective PPAR-delta agonists.[3] Grokipedia gives an EC50 of about 3.7 nM at human PPAR-delta with over 300-fold selectivity over the alpha and gamma subtypes, though Wikipedia notes that it can behave as an agonist or antagonist depending on dose and has weak activity at other nuclear receptors.[1][2]

Laboratory studies have examined GW0742 and related ligands in inflammation and cardiovascular models, including suppression of adhesion molecules in human endothelial cells and reduced angiotensin II-accelerated atherosclerosis in mice.[4][5] Other work found that PPAR ligands increased human sebum production in cultured cells, reported suppression of hepatic lipogenesis in obese diabetic mice, and examined colon carcinogenesis and cell differentiation with PPAR-beta/delta ligands.[6][7][8][9] Wikipedia lists mouse studies on pancreatitis and diet-induced hypertension.[1]

sections.h: Use in athletic and fat-loss communities
paras: Grokipedia describes anecdotal preferences, with GW0742 favoured by some for fat loss and GW501516 for endurance, and states that no human data establish either claim.[2] It reports that its analogue GW501516 promoted tumour growth in rodent studies and that long-term human safety is unknown.[2]
No studies found. Published research is limited to cell-based and animal work.[3][4][5][6][7]

timeline.event: Selective PPAR-delta agonists, including GW0742, described in a medicinal chemistry paper.[3]
